name_structures.description: A Kinyarwanda name chosen for each child, plus a given name (often a Christian name in French or English form). The Kinyarwanda name is not inherited: most Rwandans do not share a family name with their parents or siblings
name_structures.source: Kimenyi, A. (1978), 'Aspects of Naming in Kinyarwanda', Anthropological Linguistics 20(6): 258-271 (https://www.jstor.org/stable/30027411), read in full 5 Nov 2026 (copy via NYU Libraries), p. 259: no family names in Rwanda; children, father and mother each have their own name; women keep their names when married. Human Rights Watch, Leave None to Tell the Story, 1999, 'Language, Spelling and Names' (https://www.hrw.org/reports/1999/rwanda/Geno1-3-08.htm)

name_structures.description: Some accounts describe an optional third name from the father's side, or siblings' names sharing a root; others say surnames are not inherited. Unresolved: the benchmark models it as the varied parameter q (BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md §2.2)
name_structures.source: The New Times, 'Rwanda's Naming Traditions Explained', 6 May 2026 (https://allafrica.com/stories/202605070011.html), against HRW 1999 (above); RESEARCH_LOG.md, 26 Oct 2026; Kimenyi, A. (1978), 'Aspects of Naming in Kinyarwanda', Anthropological Linguistics 20(6): 258-271 (https://www.jstor.org/stable/30027411), read in full 5 Nov 2026 (copy via NYU Libraries), p. 258: the father names the child at the seventh-day ceremony (no inheritance of a name described)

name_structures.description: A child may share one name element with a parent, but never all of them
name_structures.source: Rwanda, Law No 71/2024 governing persons and family, arts 38-39 (https://www.minijust.gov.rw/fileadmin/user_upload/Minijust/Publications/Laws/OG_n___Special_of_30.07.2024_Abantu_n_umuryango.pdf), as summarised in BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md §2.2 [B1]; article text to re-read before release

order_rules.description: The national ID card has one field for names, 'Amazina/names', with no first/last split. The order of the names inside the field is not stated by this source
order_rules.source: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, RIR RWA103584.E (21 Sep 2010), 'Rwanda: Procedures for obtaining the National Identity Card…', quoting the 2008 law: card fields 'Amazina/names; Itariki yavutseho/date of birth; Igitsina/sex…' (https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/eoir/legacy/2014/10/14/RWA103584.E.pdf)

order_rules.description: In Kinyarwanda and French publications the Kinyarwanda name may come first, often in capitals (MUGISHA Jean); the capitals vary even within one publication
order_rules.source: Africana Librarians Council (ALCASA), Africana Cataloging Guidelines, '4c. Name Order' (https://africanalibrarians.wixsite.com/alcasa/6-name-order), read 5 Nov 2026: 'surnames before given names … also true elsewhere, e.g. in Rwanda – in Kinyarwanda as well as French publications'; 'often the surname is given (helpfully) all upper-case, though sometimes even that varies'

order_rules.description: In speech people are usually addressed by the given name; the Kinyarwanda name is used where a formal or identifying form is needed. A name reported orally may therefore be the given name alone
order_rules.source: No published source found (searched 5 and 9 Nov 2026: official, UN and press sources, Kimenyi 1978, Fédry 2009, Adekunle 2007). The claim was first seen on Wikipedia, 'Rwandan names', which is used only as a pointer, not as a source
order_rules.note: Hypothesis with no published source. Checked: official, UN and press sources and Kimenyi (1978) on 5 Nov 2026; Fédry (2009) and Adekunle (2007) on 9 Nov 2026 (they cover teknonymy and name taboos, not everyday use of the given name). Kimenyi (1989) and Ntahombaye (1983) exist only in print and will not be requested (user's decision, 9 Nov 2026). A field observation would settle it

order_rules.description: A parent may be called 'father/mother of X' after a child (teknonymy). In Rwanda this is documented for in-laws: a married woman may address her parents-in-law as 'the father or mother of so-and-so', using the name of their YOUNGEST child, or by praise names, or by a new name she creates. 'mama'/'papa' are also plain respectful address for any adult, so 'Mama X' may carry the person's own name: see mama-x-two-readings
order_rules.source: Adekunle, J. O. (2007), Culture and Customs of Rwanda, Westport, CT: Greenwood Press, chapter 'Gender Roles, Marriage, and Family' (taboo passage, around pp. 103-105; notes 19 and 22 on p. 114); read 9 Nov 2026 from an online copy (https://e-ihuriro.rcsprwanda.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Philosophy-Ethics-and-Rwanda-culture_-Julius-O.-Adekunle_Culture-and-Customs-of-Rwanda.pdf): 'a woman is able to address her parents-in-law as "the father or mother of so-and-so," using the name of the youngest child, or she can use the praise names of the individual' (citing Kimenyi 1989, Kinyarwanda and Kirundi Names, pp. 106-108); Fédry, J. (2009), '"Le nom, c'est l'homme"', L'Homme 191: 77-106 (https://journals.openedition.org/lhomme/22195), read 9 Nov 2026, para. 49: renaming of the parent by the child's name ('Père de Untel', 'Mère de Untel') is 'très répandu en Afrique' and usually supplants the birth name; often the eldest son or daughter, elsewhere the last child; Kraska-Szlenk, I. (2018), 'Kinship metaphors in Swahili language and culture', University of Warsaw (https://bibliotekanauki.pl/articles/462487.pdf), read 9 Nov 2026, Table 1: 'mama X' = teknonym 'X's mother' (familiar) AND 'mama X' = 'Mrs. X' (honorific); 'any adult woman can be addressed or referred to as mama', also with her own name; baba is the mirror term; the user's first-hand observation in Malawi (reported 9 Nov 2026): 'mama' and 'papa' were used by everyone to refer to a person, like 'senhora'/'senhor' (madam/sir) in Portuguese; the people there were mostly from the DRC, some from Rwanda; a Kenyan colleague of the user speaks the same way (second-hand)
order_rules.note: Rwanda-specific for in-laws (Adekunle 2007, from Kimenyi 1989); its use outside in-law address in Rwanda rests on Fédry (2009, Africa-wide) and the user's observation. Kimenyi (1989) pp. 106-108 would confirm directly

particles_and_morphemes.description: Name-initial elements described as feminine. Used ONLY to keep generated names consistent with generated sex; never to infer anyone's sex (BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md C12)
particles_and_morphemes.source: Kimenyi, A. (1978), 'Aspects of Naming in Kinyarwanda', Anthropological Linguistics 20(6): 258-271 (https://www.jstor.org/stable/30027411), read in full 5 Nov 2026 (copy via NYU Libraries), pp. 261-262: names formed with nyira-, mukaa- and kaa- are feminine; nya-, munya-, see-, nyiri-, rwaa-, ki- are possessive name-forming morphemes

particles_and_morphemes.description: Name-initial elements described as masculine. Same restriction: generation only, never inference
particles_and_morphemes.source: Kimenyi, A. (1978), 'Aspects of Naming in Kinyarwanda', Anthropological Linguistics 20(6): 258-271 (https://www.jstor.org/stable/30027411), read in full 5 Nov 2026 (copy via NYU Libraries), pp. 261-262: names formed with nyira-, mukaa- and kaa- are feminine; nya-, munya-, see-, nyiri-, rwaa-, ki- are possessive name-forming morphemes

transliteration_rules.description: Ministerial order on Kinyarwanda orthography, gazetted Oct 2014, with two years to comply; it met public pushback, so old and new spellings coexist in records. The letter-level changes are NOT yet documented here: no rule is applied until the order's text is read
transliteration_rules.source: The New Times, 29 Oct 2014 (https://www.newtimes.co.rw/article/112825/News/how-new-orthography-will-simplify-kinyarwanda) and 17 Nov 2014 (https://www.newtimes.co.rw/article/113403); Niyomugabo & Uwizeyimana (2017), Language Policy 17(3): 307-318, doi:10.1007/s10993-016-9427-x

phonetic_rules.description: [r] and [l] are one sound. Spelling uses r, except l in proper nouns that already used it and unintegrated loanwords (Kigali, Kamali). A name may be written with either letter
phonetic_rules.source: 'Phonological Aspects of Loanword Adaptation in Kinyarwanda', IJLRHSS 3(3) (http://www.ijlrhss.com/paper/volume-3-issue-3/3-HSS-598.pdf); Myers, S. (2006), 'Kinyarwanda: Introduction', Phonology: case studies, University of Texas at Austin (https://www.laits.utexas.edu/phonology/kinyarwanda/index.html), consonant table: one tap ɾ and no l; affricates pf, ts, ʧ; UN Security Council 1533 list aliases (KAKOLELE / KAKORERE; BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md [B12]): r/l alternation attested in writing
phonetic_rules.note: Wikibooks removed as a source (9 Nov 2026); the remaining source is one article in IJLRHSS, a journal of uncertain review standards. The Kirundi r/l rule (bi-kirundi r-l-one-sound) has stronger sources (Cox dictionary, official place names)

phonetic_rules.description: Vowel length and tone are not written in the official orthography; linguistic texts write long vowels doubled (aa) and tone with accents. Search forms fold both; the original form is kept (CONCEPT-IDEA.md §5.3)
phonetic_rules.source: Kinyarwanda and Kirundi Comparative Grammar (Dunwoody Press, 2007), Table 28 (https://www.matana.de/kirundi_kinyarwanda.pdf); van de Vijver, R., Uwambayinema, E. & Chuang, Y.-Y. (2024), 'Comprehension and production of Kinyarwanda verbs in the Discriminative Lexicon', Linguistics 62(1): 79-119 (doi:10.1515/ling-2021-0164), §2 Kinyarwanda phonotactics: five vowels, each short or long (citing Myers 2005); Rusanganwa, J. (2006), 'Rwanda: Language Situation', in K. Brown (ed.), Encyclopedia of Language & Linguistics, 2nd ed., Elsevier, pp. 715-716: a tone language, tone marked only in linguistic writing

phonetic_rules.description: Written glide clusters are pronounced with a stop: rw [ɾɡw], sw [skw], tw [tkw], bw [bɡ], mw [mŋ], by [bɟ], ry [ɾɟ], py [pc], ty [tc]. Spelling follows the letters, speech does not
phonetic_rules.source: FSI Kirundi Basic Course, pronunciation synopsis; Nassenstein, Modern Africa (RESEARCH_LOG.md, 28 Oct 2026); Rusanganwa, J. (2006), 'Rwanda: Language Situation', in K. Brown (ed.), Encyclopedia of Language & Linguistics, 2nd ed., Elsevier, pp. 715-716: phonetic transcription by a Rwandan linguist renders rya as [rgya] and rw'indimi as [rgwiindimi]; Nassenstein, N. (2019), Modern Africa 7(1): 11-40, p. 27 (mw for [mg], rw for [rgw], tw for [tkw]); Demolin, D. (2016), 'Clicks, stop bursts, vocoids and the timing of articulatory gestures in Kinyarwanda', Studies in African Linguistics 45(1&2), Table 1 (Jouannet 1983 transcriptions against Coupez et al. 2005 spellings; acoustic data from seven speakers), read 9 Nov 2026: written -bwá 'dog' = [ímbgá]; -rwáara = [índgwâɾà]; -nwa = [ùmùnŋwà]; -hweempwe with mp = [m̥h]
phonetic_rules.note: after removing Wikipedia, rw, ry, mw, tw and bw keep published support (Rusanganwa 2006; Nassenstein 2019); sw, by, py, ty rest on the FSI synopsis only. Raised 9 Nov 2026: four published sources agree (Rusanganwa 2006, Nassenstein 2019, Demolin 2016, FSI)

phonetic_rules.description: After m, the letter p stands for an aspirated [h]: impamvu [imhamvu]
phonetic_rules.source: Kinyarwanda and Kirundi Comparative Grammar (Zorc & Nibagwire, Dunwoody Press, 2007) (https://www.matana.de/kirundi_kinyarwanda.pdf), §2 (compensatory lengthening): /mp'aamafaraanga/ 'Give me some money!' < /n-h-a ama-faraanga/: written mp stands for n + h; Demolin, D. (2016), 'Clicks, stop bursts, vocoids and the timing of articulatory gestures in Kinyarwanda', Studies in African Linguistics 45(1&2), Table 1 (Jouannet 1983 transcriptions against Coupez et al. 2005 spellings; acoustic data from seven speakers), read 9 Nov 2026: written -bwá 'dog' = [ímbgá]; -rwáara = [índgwâɾà]; -nwa = [ùmùnŋwà]; -hweempwe with mp = [m̥h]

phonetic_rules.description: Chichewa and Chitumbuka spelling has one accented letter, ŵ (standardised 1973). A Malawian writer may use it; search forms fold ŵ to w, and the original is kept
phonetic_rules.source: UK Government, Malawi Toponymic Factfile, 2025, 'Languages' (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68aee2f02f1856648215588f/Malawi_Toponymic_Factfile.pdf), read 5 Nov 2026

common_administrative_forms.description: Kinyarwanda name in capitals before the given name (MUGISHA Jean). Capitals mark which element is the Kinyarwanda name; case is kept in the source value and folded only in search forms
common_administrative_forms.source: Africana Librarians Council (ALCASA), Africana Cataloging Guidelines, '4c. Name Order' (https://africanalibrarians.wixsite.com/alcasa/6-name-order), read 5 Nov 2026

spelling_conventions.note: written ny before vowels, n before consonants (nchi)

spellings: l after a, o or u
l at the start of a word (no Chichewa word begins with r)
r for l after i or e (hypercorrection)
spelling_conventions.note: Sourced: the writing rule (Chirwa 2008, from the Chichewa Orthography Rules; 1973 date from the UK factfile). Hypothesis, not sourced: that Malawian clerks apply it to refugees' names (word-initial l: Rukundo as Lukundo; after a/o/u: Nkurunziza as Nkulunziza; hypercorrect r after i/e)
spelling_conventions.source: Chirwa, M. N. (2008), 'Trill maintenance and replacement in Chichewa: a study on newsreaders' speech from three radio stations in Malawi', MA dissertation, University of Cape Town (http://hdl.handle.net/11427/10191), read 9 Nov 2026: pp. 4-5 and 31, citing Mchombo (2001) and the Chichewa Orthography Rules: [r] and [l] are allophones of one phoneme; <r> is written after the front vowels i and e, <l> after a, o and u, within a morpheme; no Chichewa word begins with r; in speech the trill is often replaced by [l], and writers unsure of the rule hypercorrect (ndili misspelled ndiri); UK Government, Malawi Toponymic Factfile (2025), 'Languages' (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68aee2f02f1856648215588f/Malawi_Toponymic_Factfile.pdf): 'The orthography of Chichewa was standardised in 1973 in the New Chichewa Orthography Rules'

spelling_conventions.note: Chichewa Board spelling writes ch (and tch when aspirated), never c alone, so a Malawian clerk may write a c-name as ch (Ciza as Chiza); that clerks do so with refugees' names is a hypothesis
spelling_conventions.source: Peace Corps Malawi, 'An Introduction to the Chichewa Language' ('The letter C always carries an H'; no Q or X) (https://files.peacecorps.gov/multimedia/audio/languagelessons/malawi/MW_Chichewa_Language_Lessons.pdf), read 5 Nov 2026; Downing, L. J. & Mtenje, A. (2017), The Phonology of Chichewa, Oxford University Press, ch. 1, note 2 (publisher preview, https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780191037733_A30389705/preview-9780191037733_A30389705.pdf), read 9 Nov 2026: the Chichewa Board's convention writes the unaspirated affricate as ch and the aspirated one as tch; earlier work (Watkins 1937) and some linguists write c

(2016), 'Clicks, stop bursts, vocoids and the timing of articulatory gestures in Kinyarwanda', Studies in African Linguistics 45(1&2), Table 1 (Jouannet 1983 transcriptions against Coupez et al. 2005 spellings; acoustic data from seven speakers), read 9 Nov 2026: written -bwá 'dog' = [ímbgá]; -rwáara = [índgwâɾà]; -nwa = [ùmùnŋwà]; -hweempwe with mp = [m̥h]; Nassenstein (2019), p. 27 note 14: written 'bg' in at least one Kinyarwanda variety of eastern DRC

relationship_implications.note: Different Kinyarwanda names are expected among parents, children and siblings, so disagreement is no evidence against kinship. Agreement may be coincidence (common names) or the optional father element; accounts conflict (structure-father-element)
relationship_implications.source: HRW 1999; Law 71/2024 arts 38-39; The New Times, 6 May 2026

known_failure_modes.description: Systems with first/last fields split the single Amazina field in either order; MUGISHA Jean may be stored with Mugisha as first or last name. Compare across both orders
The Christian given name changes form with the writer's language (Jean / John / Yohana); handled by the cross-pack given-name data (week 4)
Pre- and post-2014 spellings, and the official orthography not being followed, give several written forms of one name (Uwimana / Uwimanna)
Names written by a clerk who hears the spoken form follow the sounds, not the spelling (rw as rgw, r as l); see listener_confusions
The same name in Kirundi spelling (Habyarimana / Havyarimana: by → vy, cy → c, jy → j, shy → sh); the rules belong to the bi-kirundi pack
Inferring sex from feminine or masculine prefixes is forbidden; a match is never scored up or down on it

A child may not say, or not know, a parent's own name, because children do not call parents by name; expect kin terms or 'Mama X'/'Papa X' instead, whose X may be the parent's own name or a sibling's (mama-x-two-readings). In Rwanda the avoidance also covers parents-in-law. Retrieval must not require the parent's full own name
known_failure_modes.source: Fédry, J. (2009), '"Le nom, c'est l'homme"', L'Homme 191: 77-106 (https://journals.openedition.org/lhomme/22195), read 9 Nov 2026, para. 55: in Africa generally the child does not call father or mother by name; in many places, Rwanda named, this also applies to parents-in-law

known_failure_modes.description: A Rwandan child under about 15 may be reluctant to say their own name, as part of an upbringing in modesty; a minor who gives no name, or only a nickname, is not evidence of a false or hidden identity
known_failure_modes.source: Fédry, J. (2009), '"Le nom, c'est l'homme"', L'Homme 191: 77-106 (https://journals.openedition.org/lhomme/22195), read 9 Nov 2026, para. 63: 'Au Rwanda, on ne dit pas son propre nom avant la fin de la croissance physique, vers 15 ans (ntaw'igura agikura)'; the article cites personal communications (Ganza 2002; Mbonimpa), so treat as low confidence

known_failure_modes.description: 'Mama X' / 'Papa X' is ambiguous: X may be the person's OWN name (respectful address, like 'Mrs. X') or the name of their CHILD (teknonym, 'X's mother'). Search both readings: X as a given name of the sought adult, and X as a child of the sought adult. 'Mama'/'Papa' alone does not show that the person is anyone's parent
known_failure_modes.source: the user's first-hand observation in Malawi (reported 9 Nov 2026): 'mama' and 'papa' were used by everyone to refer to a person, like 'senhora'/'senhor' (madam/sir) in Portuguese; the people there were mostly from the DRC, some from Rwanda; a Kenyan colleague of the user speaks the same way (second-hand) (field observation, not a published source; a Rwanda-specific publication, e.g. Kimenyi 1989, would let it be cited); Swahili evidence: Kraska-Szlenk, I. (2018), 'Kinship metaphors in Swahili language and culture', University of Warsaw (https://bibliotekanauki.pl/articles/462487.pdf), read 9 Nov 2026, Table 1: 'mama X' = teknonym 'X's mother' (familiar) AND 'mama X' = 'Mrs. X' (honorific); 'any adult woman can be addressed or referred to as mama', also with her own name; baba is the mirror term

known_failure_modes.description: Traditionally a married Rwandan woman does not say the names of her husband or her parents-in-law (taboo gutsinda), and does not call her husband's brothers, sisters or cousins by their first names. A wife searching for a missing husband, or giving his relatives' names, may use a teknonym, a praise name or a kin term, or ask someone else to say the name. Intake must accept that, and the reporter's reluctance is not a sign of a false claim. Many such taboos are weaker today
known_failure_modes.source: Adekunle, J. O. (2007), Culture and Customs of Rwanda, Westport, CT: Greenwood Press, chapter 'Gender Roles, Marriage, and Family' (taboo passage, around pp. 103-105; notes 19 and 22 on p. 114); read 9 Nov 2026 from an online copy (https://e-ihuriro.rcsprwanda.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Philosophy-Ethics-and-Rwanda-culture_-Julius-O.-Adekunle_Culture-and-Customs-of-Rwanda.pdf): a wife 'was prohibited from calling her husband's brothers, sisters, or cousins by their first names'; 'Under no circumstances would a woman call her parents-in-law by name. This taboo is called gutsinda (when women are not allowed to name their husbands)'; 'many aspects of the traditional culture, especially the taboos on women, are no longer applicable' (section taken from Kimenyi, A. (1978), 'An Ethnolinguistic Analysis of Kinyarwanda Kinship Terms', Sixth Annual Meeting of the California Linguistic Association)
